chapters.title: Tablet I — He Who Saw the Deep
paragraphs: Let me tell you the story of Gilgamesh — the man who knew everything. He had seen every land in the world and witnessed every kind of wisdom. He understood mysteries and uncovered what was hidden. He brought back knowledge from before the Great Flood. He traveled roads so distant they left him exhausted. And when he returned, he carved the whole story into standing stones for all to read.

When the gods shaped Gilgamesh, they gave him a perfect form. The sun god Shamash granted him glory. Adad, the fearsome storm god, gave him courage. The great gods made his magnificence surpass all others — terrifying as a great wild bull. Two-thirds god they made him. One-third man.

He built the great rampart of Uruk and the wall of the sacred Eanna temple, Ishtar's holy sanctuary. Look at the outer walls — they gleam like copper. See the inner wall — nothing can rival it. Touch the threshold stone. It dates from ancient times. Enter the Eanna temple, the dwelling of Ishtar, which no later king or living person could ever equal. Climb up and walk along the wall of Uruk. Inspect the cornerstone. Examine the brickwork. See if the wall is not made of fired brick, its foundation laid by the Seven Sages. One-third of Uruk is city. One-third is garden. One-third is field. And there is a precinct for the temple of Ishtar. These parts and the precinct make up the whole of Uruk. Open the copper tablet box. Unlatch the clasp of its bronze lock. Unbind the fastenings of its hidden opening. Bring out and read the lapis lazuli tablet that tells of the great hardships Gilgamesh endured.

Greater than other kings, towering in stature, he was a hero born in Uruk — a wild and rampaging bull. He marched at the front as leader. He brought up the rear as a trusted companion. He was a great net protecting his people, a surging flood-wave that could devastate even walls of stone. Son of Lugalbanda, Gilgamesh was perfection in strength. Son also of the noble cow-goddess Ninsun. He was tall, glorious, and terrifying. He cut open passes through the mountains. He dug wells on mountain slopes. He crossed the great ocean to meet the sunrise, searching every corner of the world for the secret of life. By his strength alone, he reached Utnapishtim the distant. He restored the holy places the Flood had destroyed. For all of humankind, he established the sacred rites of heaven.

Who could rival Gilgamesh? Who else could say, 'I am the king'? From the moment of his birth, his name was destined to be Gilgamesh. Two-thirds god they made him. One-third man. The Great Goddess herself designed his body. Nudimmud bestowed glory, beauty, and perfection upon him. His foot was a triple cubit in size, his leg half a rod. Six cubits he covered in each stride. His cheeks were full with a thick beard, and his hair was dense as barley. His beauty was beyond comparison. He was the most handsome man on earth.

Around the enclosed space of Uruk he walked, mighty as a wild bull with his head held high. No one could challenge him with weapons. His men stood at attention, longing for his commands. But the old men of Uruk complained that Gilgamesh had left no son to his father, because his arrogance had grown boundless. He had taken all their children. Was Gilgamesh not supposed to be the shepherd of his people? He did not leave a daughter to her mother, nor a maiden to her warrior, nor a wife to her husband. And yet — Gilgamesh was the magnificent and glorious shepherd of his people.

The gods heard the people's cries. The gods of heaven called upon Anu, lord of Uruk: 'His men stand at attention, longing for his commands. Gilgamesh has left no son to his father. His arrogance has grown boundless. He has taken all their children — is Gilgamesh not the shepherd of his people? He does not leave a daughter to her mother, nor a maiden to her warrior, nor a wife to her husband.'

Anu heard the gods' lament. They cried out to Aruru, the goddess: 'Aruru, you created Gilgamesh. Now create a rival for him, someone to match him in strength. Let them contend with each other so that Uruk might have peace.' When she heard these words, Aruru formed an image of Anu in her mind. She washed her hands and broke off a piece of clay, then cast it on the ground. In this way she created Enkidu, the hero. His entire body was covered with hair. He wore his hair long, like a woman. It grew thick and luxuriant, like that of Nisaba, the grain goddess. He knew nothing of the land or its people. He was clothed like the god of the wild. He ate herbs alongside gazelles. He drank at the watering hole with the animals. Among the creatures of the water, his heart was glad.

At the watering place, Enkidu encountered a trapper — on the first day, then the second, then the third. Each time, the two came face to face. When the trapper saw Enkidu, he went pale with fear. He took his animals and retreated home. Stiff with fright, numb with terror, his heart pounding wildly. Fear filled him to the core, and his face looked like that of a man who had traveled a great distance. The trapper spoke to his father: 'A man unlike any other has come down from the mountains. His strength is beyond anything I have seen. He is like an immortal. He roams through all the mountains. He regularly feeds with the animals and drinks at my watering place. But I was too afraid to approach him. He has filled the pits I dug. He has destroyed the nets I set. He has let all the cattle and wild beasts escape from my hands. He will not let me hunt.'

His father spoke to the trapper: 'My son, in Uruk there lives a man named Gilgamesh. No one is stronger than he. He is like a star fallen from the highest heaven. Go to Uruk and tell Gilgamesh about the strength of this wild man. Ask him to give you the temple woman Shamhat. Take her with you. When the animals come down to drink, let her remove her clothing and reveal her body. Enkidu will see her and come to her. Then the animals that grew up with him in the wild will abandon him.'

The trapper followed his father's advice and traveled to Uruk. He entered the city and found Gilgamesh. He said to him: 'A man unlike any other has come down from the mountains. His strength is beyond anything I have seen. He is like an immortal. He roams through all the mountains. He regularly feeds with the animals and drinks at my watering place. But I was too afraid to approach him. He has filled the pits I dug. He has destroyed the nets I set. He has let all the cattle and wild beasts escape from my hands. He will not let me hunt.' Gilgamesh replied: 'Go, trapper, and bring the temple woman Shamhat with you. When the animals come down to drink, let her remove her clothing and reveal her body. Enkidu will see her and come to her. Then the animals that grew up with him in the wild will abandon him.'

The trapper departed and took the temple woman Shamhat with him. They took the straight road and reached the appointed place on the third day. The trapper and Shamhat hid themselves. For one day, then two, they waited by the watering place. The animals came to drink. Enkidu arrived among them — born of the mountains, eating herbs with the gazelles, drinking alongside the beasts. His heart rejoiced among the creatures of the water. When the trapper caught sight of him, he whispered: 'That is he, Shamhat! Loosen your garments. Uncover yourself so that he may see you. Do not hesitate — take hold of his attention. He will see you and come to you. Open your garments and let him lie in your arms. Give him pleasure in the way of women. Then the animals that grew up with him in the wild will abandon him while he holds you in his embrace.'

Shamhat loosened her garments. She uncovered herself. She did not hesitate, and she captured his attention. She opened her garment, and he lay in her arms. She gave him pleasure in the way of women, and he held her in his embrace.

For six days and six nights, Enkidu stayed with Shamhat. After he had satisfied himself, he turned to look for his animals. The gazelles looked at him and turned away. The beasts of the field retreated from him. Enkidu was startled. His body grew weak. His knees stiffened as his animals departed, and he was less agile than before. But as he listened, something shifted inside him. He turned back to Shamhat, drawn to her, and gazed into her face. She spoke to him and said: 'You are noble, Enkidu. You could be like a god. Why do you lie down with the beasts of the field? Come — I will take you to the great walled city of Uruk, to the glorious temple of Anu and Ishtar, to the palace of Gilgamesh, the hero who is perfect in strength, who surpasses all men in power like a mountain bull.'

Her words entered his heart, and he longed for a friend. Enkidu spoke to Shamhat: 'Come then, take me and lead me to that glorious dwelling, the sacred seat of Anu and Ishtar, to the palace of Gilgamesh, the hero perfect in strength, who surpasses all men like a mountain bull. I will challenge him. I will declare in Uruk that I am the mighty one. Let me enter the city, and I will upend the order of things. I will show that the mightiest man is the one who was born in the wilderness.'

Shamhat said to Enkidu: 'Then let us go to Gilgamesh, so he can look upon you. I will lead you to him, for I know where he will be. Look at Uruk, Enkidu — see the people in their finery, celebrating every day with some holiday. The lyre and drum never stop playing. Beautiful women stand in their radiance, ripe and merry, always ready for the pleasures of the night. Enkidu, you do not yet know how to live like a civilized man. Let me show you Gilgamesh, a man overflowing with feeling. Look at his face — it glows with heroic courage. He has magnificent strength throughout his whole body. His power is greater than yours. He never rests, not by day or night. Enkidu, change your hostile thoughts.
Shamash loves Gilgamesh. Anu, Enlil, and Ea whisper wisdom into his ear. Before you even came down from the mountains, Gilgamesh already saw you in a dream in Uruk.'

Gilgamesh went to understand the dream. He said to his mother: 'Mother, I had a dream last night. The stars of heaven fell upon me like a host sent by Anu. I bore this weight and it grew heavy. I became weak and could not carry it. All of Uruk gathered around it. The heroes kissed its feet. They stood me up. I carried it and brought it to you.'

The mother of Gilgamesh, who knows all things, spoke to her son: 'Someone, Gilgamesh, who like you was born in the wild, and whom the mountains raised — when you see him, you will rejoice as a woman rejoices. Heroes will kiss his feet. You will spare him and try to bring him to me.'

Gilgamesh slept and saw another dream, which he told to his mother: 'Mother, I have seen another dream. My likeness appeared in the streets of Uruk, in the plazas. An axe was brandished, and people gathered around it. The axe made him fierce. I saw him and I rejoiced. I loved him as I would love a woman. I embraced him. I took him and made him my brother.'
The mother of Gilgamesh, who knows all things, spoke to her son: 'Gilgamesh, the man you saw, the one you embraced like a woman — it means he will be your companion.' Gilgamesh understood the dream.

chapters.title: Tablet II — The Taming of Enkidu
paragraphs: Enkidu sat before the woman. He embraced her body and opened himself to her. For six days and seven nights, Enkidu lay with the temple woman. He forgot the place where he was born.

Shamhat spoke to Enkidu: 'I look at you, Enkidu, and you are like a god. Why do you roam the fields with cattle? Come, let me lead you to Uruk, to the holy temple of Anu. Arise, Enkidu — let me take you to the dwelling of Anu, the place where Gilgamesh lives, perfect in vitality. You will embrace him like a wife. You will love him like yourself. Come, get up from the ground and find your place.'

He listened to her words and accepted her counsel. She stripped off one garment and dressed him in it. She kept the other for herself. She took his hand and led him like a god to the fertile meadow where the sheepfolds stood. There the shepherds received them and offered food. They spoke of Enkidu — born in the mountains, accustomed to eating herbs with the gazelles, drinking water with the cattle, and finding joy among the creatures of the water. He had always sucked the milk of wild cattle. They placed bread before him. He broke a piece off and stared at it in confusion. Enkidu had never eaten bread before. He had never been taught to drink ale.
Shamhat spoke to Enkidu: 'Eat the food, Enkidu — it is the sustenance of life. Drink the ale — it is the custom of the land.'

Enkidu ate food until he was full. He drank seven goblets of ale. His spirit loosened. He grew cheerful. His heart became glad and his face shone. A barber removed the hair from his body. He was anointed with oil. He became like a civilized man. He put on a garment and looked like any other man. He took up his weapon and attacked lions, so the shepherds could rest at night. He plunged his dagger into them and overcame them all. The great shepherds lay down in peace — Enkidu was their protector. The strong man, the unique hero, stayed awake to guard them.

A certain man had been invited to a wedding in Uruk. Enkidu was making love to Shamhat when he looked up and saw the man. He said to Shamhat: 'Bring that man closer. Why has he come? I want to know his purpose.'
The woman called to the man. He approached and Enkidu studied him. 'Where are you going? Why does your journey seem so burdensome?'

The man opened his mouth and spoke to Enkidu: 'I have been invited to a wedding, because marriage is the destiny of men. I will fill the wedding table with delicious food for the feast. But in Uruk, it is the king who goes first. Gilgamesh, the King of Uruk, claims the right to sleep with the bride before the bridegroom. This was decreed by the gods. From the cutting of his umbilical cord, this has been his fate.'
When Enkidu heard this, his face went pale.
(About nine lines missing.)

Enkidu walked at the front and Shamhat followed behind. He entered Uruk and people gathered around him. As he stood in the streets, the men said to one another: 'He looks like Gilgamesh in form — though shorter in stature and thicker in bone. Surely this is the one who was born in the highlands and raised on the milk of wild cattle.'
In Uruk, the customary festivals and sacrifices were underway. The young men rejoiced and set up a champion. They found in Enkidu a rival for Gilgamesh — a hero of fine appearance, like a god.

For the goddess Ishtar, a couch had been prepared. Gilgamesh lay down, and afterward in the night he went to meet the maiden bride. Enkidu stepped into the street and blocked Gilgamesh's path during his display of power.

All of Uruk surrounded Gilgamesh. The people gathered around him. A crowd assembled to watch. All the men bowed down and kissed his feet. For Ishtar a couch was prepared, and Gilgamesh, godlike, was made the substitute.

Enkidu advanced toward him, hair flowing luxuriantly. They met in the plaza. Enkidu blocked the gate to the wedding house with his foot, refusing to let Gilgamesh enter. They seized each other like oxen. They fought. The threshold crumbled. The wall cracked. They grappled and struggled. The threshold crumbled. The wall cracked. Finally Gilgamesh braced his foot against the ground, and his fury subsided. His rage cooled. When it did, Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Your mother bore you as a unique being. Ninsun, the wild cow of the stall, has raised your head above all men. Enlil has decreed kingship over men for you.'
Enkidu said to Gilgamesh: 'Why do you want to do this thing that is so difficult? Why do you desire to go down to the forest?' They kissed one another and became bonded in friendship.
[In a missing section, Gilgamesh introduces Enkidu to his mother.]
'He is the mightiest in all the land, possessed of great strength. No one is stronger than he. He is like a star from the highest heaven. He is tall in stature, like a battlement.'
The mother of Gilgamesh, who knows everything, spoke to her son: 'Enkidu has neither family nor kin. With flowing hair like a woman, he was born in the wild and has no brothers.'

Enkidu's eyes filled with tears. He clutched his heart and sighed sadly. His eyes filled with tears again. He clutched his heart and sighed. Gilgamesh looked at him with concern and said: 'My friend, why are your eyes filled with tears? Why do you clutch your heart and sigh so sadly?'
Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'The fighting has exhausted my strength. My arms are weak. My power has drained away.'
Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'There is Humbaba, the terrible one. Let us destroy him and end his power. Let us go to the cedar forest and make Humbaba tremble in his lair.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, know that when I lived in the mountains, I traveled into the heart of the forest to a distance of one double-hour among the cattle. But who would dare to penetrate it all the way to Humbaba? His roar is a flood. His mouth is fire. His breath is death. Why do you want to do this — to advance toward Humbaba's dwelling?'
Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'I will climb the slopes of the forest to Humbaba's dwelling. I will go into the forest.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'How can we venture to the home of Humbaba and protect the cedar forest? Enlil has appointed him as guardian — a sevenfold terror. His voice is the Deluge. His speech is fire. His breath is death. He can hear every movement in the forest from a great distance. Who would dare enter his forest? Adad may be first among storms, but Humbaba is second. Not even the Igigi gods would oppose him. Enlil decreed him to be a sevenfold terror. To enter his forest is to be seized by trembling.'

Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'Whoever overcomes terror, my friend — Shamash will bless him with long life. People will speak of it at the gates. Wherever terror must be faced, you shrink from death. Your courage lacks strength. I will go ahead of you, even though you cry out that I should be afraid. If I fall before Humbaba, I will have established my name. People will say that Gilgamesh fell fighting the terrible Humbaba. You were born in the wilderness. The lion feared you. You know all of this. When you call out to me, you weaken my heart. But I am determined. I will enter the cedar forest. I will make my name. Let us have the artisans forge our weapons.'

They gave the work to the artisans, who sat together at the forge. The masters molded hatchets — axes weighing three talents each. They molded lances with blades of two talents, and spears of thirty minas attached to them. The hilts of the lances held thirty minas of gold. Gilgamesh and Enkidu were each equipped with ten talents of weaponry.
Gilgamesh sealed shut all seven gates of Uruk. He assembled the people in the street of Uruk, where he took his throne. In the street, the people sat before him. He spoke to the elders of Uruk:

'Hear me, elders of Uruk! I will walk the path to the terrible Humbaba, whose name fills every land. I will conquer him in the cedar forest, like a strong son of Uruk. I will make the whole land hear that I am determined to conquer him. I will establish a name for myself.'

To the young men of Uruk, Gilgamesh said: 'Hear me, young men of Uruk! You who know combat — I will walk the path to the terrible Humbaba and face him in battle. Give me your blessings, that I may see you again and return safely to Uruk. When I come back, I will celebrate the New Year twice over, two times in one year. Let the rejoicing begin and the drums beat out in honor of Ninsun!'

Enkidu spoke to the elders and the young men: 'Tell Gilgamesh that he must not go to the cedar forest. Its guardian is a power that never rests. Humbaba — his voice is the Deluge, his speech is fire, his breath is death. He can hear every movement in the forest from a great distance. Who would enter his forest? Adad may be first among storms, but Humbaba is second. Not even the Igigi gods would oppose him. Enlil decreed him to be a sevenfold terror. To enter his forest is to be seized by trembling.'

The elders of Uruk brought word to Gilgamesh: 'You are young, Gilgamesh, and your heart carries you away. You do not know what you propose to do. We hear that Humbaba is enraged. Who has ever opposed his weapon? To one double-hour into the heart of the forest — who has ever gone that far? Humbaba, whose roar is a deluge, whose mouth is fire, whose breath is death. Why do you want to do this? To advance toward Humbaba's dwelling?'
Gilgamesh heard the advice of his counselors. He looked at his friend and said: 'Now, my friend — I fear him, but I will go to the cedar forest. I will go with you to the cedar forest.'

chapters.title: Tablet III — Preparations for the Journey
paragraphs: Gilgamesh spoke to the elders of Uruk: 'I, Gilgamesh, the strong one of the land, will take a road I have never walked. When I have succeeded, I will praise you with a joyful heart. I will honor your power and seat you on thrones.'
The masters brought the weapons — bow and quiver placed in hand. Gilgamesh took his hatchet and his quiver. With his lance in his belt, he and Enkidu prepared to set out.

The elders of Uruk approached Gilgamesh. 'How long until you return to Uruk?' Then they counseled him for the road: 'Do not rely on your strength alone, Gilgamesh! Save your food and pace yourself. Let Enkidu go before you. He knows the way. He has walked the road to the entrance of Humbaba's forest. The one who goes first will protect his companion. Guard his path and guard yourself. May Shamash carry out your goal. May he let your eyes see the prophecy of your mouth. May he find for you the hidden path. May he level the road for your feet and the mountain for your step. During the night, may comforting words reach you. May Lugalbanda stand by you in your task. Like a young man, may he fulfill your goal. Wash your feet in the river of Humbaba. Dig a well nearby. May there always be pure water for your offerings, and goblets of water poured out to Shamash. May Lugalbanda take note.'
The elders of Uruk spoke to Enkidu: 'We place our king Gilgamesh in your care. Bring him back to us and return him safely.'
Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'Come, my friend. Let us go to the Great Palace, to the great Queen Ninsun. Ninsun, who knows all things, will set our feet on the path of wise counsel.'
Hand in hand, Gilgamesh and Enkidu went to the Great Palace, to the great Queen Ninsun. Gilgamesh rose and entered her presence.

Gilgamesh spoke to Ninsun: 'Ninsun, I am going to the entrance of Humbaba's forest. I will face a war I do not know. I will travel a road I have never walked. Give me your blessing. Let me see your face again safely and return through the gates of Uruk. When I come back, I will celebrate the New Year twice over, two times in one year. Let the rejoicing begin and the drums beat out in honor of Ninsun.'

Ninsun, the wild cow, listened intently and sadly to the words of Gilgamesh, her son, and to Enkidu as well. She put on a beautiful gown to adorn her body and chose a diadem for her breast. She placed her crown and tiara on her head. Before Shamash she made a smoke offering and poured out a drink, then lifted her hands in prayer: 'Why have you given my son Gilgamesh such a restless heart? Now you have set him on a distant road to Humbaba. He goes toward an unknown fight, an unknown war. From the day he leaves until the day he returns — until he reaches the great cedar forest, until he kills Humbaba the tyrant and removes that horror from the land that you detest — let your bride Aya the fearless remind you each day to entrust Gilgamesh to the stars, the watchers of the night.'

'You who opened the gates for the herds to escape — the heavens brighten for you and the animals await your rosy light. Let your bride Aya remind you to entrust Gilgamesh to the stars, the watchers of the night. Make the days long and the nights short while Gilgamesh walks the road to the Cedar Forest. Let him be resolute. Let him make camp at nightfall. On the day Gilgamesh and Enkidu battle Humbaba, unleash all the winds — south, north, east, and west, the hurricane, the tempest, the typhoon, the gale, the frost-wind, the devil-wind, the blast and counterblast, and the tornado. Let thirteen winds darken Humbaba's face so Gilgamesh may reach him with his weapons. When your own flames are kindled, O Shamash, turn your face toward your faithful one. Your swift mules shall carry you. A restful bed shall be yours. The gods, your brothers, shall bring you food. Aya the bride shall dry your face with her robe.'

Ninsun pleaded again to Shamash: 'O Shamash, will Gilgamesh not share the heavens with you? Will he not share royal honors with the moon? Will he not become as wise as Ea of the deep sea, or rule the people with Irnina? Will he not dwell in the afterlife with Ningishzida?'

After Ninsun had finished her plea to Shamash, she put out her censer, came down from the roof, and spoke to Enkidu: 'Enkidu, although you were not born from my womb, from this day forward your people will be among the devotees of Gilgamesh — the priestesses and the women of the temple.' She placed the sacred symbols around Enkidu's neck. 'The priestesses accept the foundling. The women of the temple raise him as a foster child. Enkidu, whom I love — I take you as my own son. Enkidu shall be brother to Gilgamesh. When you walk together to the Cedar Forest, let the days be long and the nights short. Be resolute. Make camp at nightfall.'
[A damaged section describes the rituals Gilgamesh and Enkidu perform to guarantee safe passage. When the text resumes, Gilgamesh is giving instructions for governing Uruk in his absence.]

'From the day I leave until I return — until I reach the great cedar forest, until I kill Humbaba the tyrant and remove that horror which Shamash detests — do not gather the young men in the streets or pass judgment on the lawsuits of the weak while we are fighting Humbaba.'
The elders and the young men offered their blessings to Gilgamesh. The young men gathered around him. The elders kissed his feet and said:

'Do not rely on your strength alone, Gilgamesh! Save your food and pace yourself. Let Enkidu go before you. He knows the way. He has walked the road to the entrance of Humbaba's forest. The one who goes first will protect his companion. Guard his path and guard yourself. May Shamash carry out your goal. May he let your eyes see the prophecy of your mouth. May he find for you the hidden path. May he level the road for your feet and the mountain for your step. During the night, may comforting words reach you. May Lugalbanda stand by you in your task. Like a young man, may he fulfill your goal. Wash your feet in the river of Humbaba. Dig a well nearby. May there always be pure water for your offerings, and goblets of water poured out to Shamash. May Lugalbanda take note.'
The elders of Uruk spoke to Enkidu: 'We place our king Gilgamesh in your care. Bring him back to us and return him safely.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Since you are determined to take the road, do not let your heart be afraid. Trust me. Keep your eyes on me. In the forest, I came to know Humbaba's home. Send the crowd back — they must not come with us.'
The assembled men heard Enkidu's words and returned to their homes with joyful hearts. The young men raised a prayer to Shamash: 'May the god go before you. May Shamash bring you success.'
Gilgamesh and Enkidu set forth.

chapters.title: Tablet IV — The Journey to the Cedar Forest
paragraphs: At twenty leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty leagues they stopped to rest. They walked for six weeks, drawing ever closer to Mount Lebanon. Before Shamash they dug a hole. Gilgamesh climbed to the top of a hill and poured his offering into the hole, saying: 'Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see dream-visions, O Shamash.'

Enkidu built a shelter for the God of Dreams. A great wind chilled them. Enkidu hung a covering while Gilgamesh rested his chin on his knees and fell asleep. In the middle of the night, he woke and spoke to his friend: 'Did you call me? Why have I woken? Did you touch me? Has a god passed by? Why are my muscles trembling? Enkidu, my friend, I had a dream. A terrible dream. We were walking in the valleys between the mountains, and a great mountain fell down upon us.'

Enkidu heard the dream and said: 'My friend, this dream is favorable. It tells us we will triumph over Humbaba. The mountain you saw is Humbaba. The dream foretells that we will kill him and leave his corpse in the wasteland. Come morning, Shamash will send us a good omen.'

At twenty leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty leagues they stopped to rest. They walked for six weeks, drawing ever closer to Mount Lebanon. Before Shamash they dug a hole. Gilgamesh climbed to the top of a hill and poured his offering into the hole, saying: 'Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see dream-visions, O Shamash.'

Enkidu built a shelter for the God of Dreams. A great wind chilled them. Enkidu hung a covering while Gilgamesh rested his chin on his knees and fell asleep. In the middle of the night, he woke and spoke to his friend: 'Did you call me? Why have I woken? Did you touch me? Has a god passed by? Why are my muscles trembling? Enkidu, my friend, I had another dream. A terrible dream. Heaven thundered. Earth shook. Day turned to darkness. Lightning struck. Fire blazed, thick with destruction and death. Then suddenly the light faded. The fire went out and turned to smoke. You were born in the wilderness. What do you make of it?'

Enkidu heard the dream and said: 'My friend, this dream is favorable. We are drawing close to the forest. You will soon see the radiance of the god Humbaba, whom you fear. Like a bull you will batter him and bring him to his knees. The old man you saw is your god Lugalbanda. Come morning, Shamash will send us a good omen.'

At twenty leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty leagues they stopped to rest. They walked for six weeks, drawing ever closer to Mount Lebanon. Before Shamash they dug a hole. Gilgamesh climbed to the top of a hill and poured his offering into the hole, saying: 'Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see dream-visions, O Shamash.'
