In the middle of the night, he woke and spoke to his friend: 'Did you call me? Why have I woken? Did you touch me? Has a god passed by? Why are my muscles trembling? Enkidu, my friend, I had another dream. A terrible dream. I saw a Thunderbird in the sky. It flew like a cloud. Its mouth was fire and its breath was death. A strange man stood before me, and the bird seized my arm in its talons......'

Enkidu heard the dream and said: 'My friend, this dream is favorable. You dreamed of a Thunderbird in the sky. It flew like a cloud. Its mouth was fire and its breath was death. A strange man stood before you and the bird seized your arm in its talons. The man you saw was Shamash. We will bring about the destruction of Humbaba. We will bind his wings. Come morning, Shamash will send us a good omen.'

At twenty leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty leagues they stopped to rest. They walked for six weeks. Before Shamash they dug a hole. Gilgamesh climbed to the top of a hill and poured his offering into the hole, saying: 'Mountain, bring me a dream. Let me see dream-visions, O Shamash.'

Enkidu built a shelter for the God of Dreams. A great wind chilled them. Enkidu hung a covering while Gilgamesh rested his chin on his knees and fell asleep. In the middle of the night, he woke and spoke to his friend: 'Did you call me? Why have I woken? Did you touch me? Has a god passed by? Why are my muscles trembling? Enkidu, my friend, I had another dream. A terrible dream. I grappled with a wild bull that pounded the ground to dust. I fell to my knees before the bull, and it gave me water to drink from its water-skin.'

Enkidu heard the dream and said: 'My friend, the god we go to face is not the wild bull. Shamash is the wild bull, and he protects us both. The one who gave you water is Lugalbanda, who brings honor to you. We must join together to accomplish a great deed — something that has never been done before. Come morning, Shamash will send us a good omen.'
At the entrance to the forest, Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Why are you weeping? Son of Uruk, stand tall!'

Shamash heard and sent a booming voice from the sky: 'Hurry! Stand against Humbaba! Do not let him enter the forest. Do not let him reach his grove. He must not put on the seven cloaks. He wears one, but six he has shed.'
Humbaba let out a mighty roar. His voice was like thunder. The forest shook with his bellowing. He sounded like Adad, the God of the Storm.

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My arms grow stiff and my knees are shaking.' Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'Why should we talk like cowards? Did we not cross the mighty mountains? Do not be afraid. Let your voice ring out like a drum. Let the stiffness leave your arms and the shaking leave your knees. Take my hand and let us go forward. Turn your thoughts to battle. Forget death and think about life. The one who goes first will protect his companion. Guard his path and guard yourself.'
The two men arrived at the Cedar Forest. They stopped speaking and stood still.

chapters.title: Tablet V — The Battle with Humbaba
paragraphs: There they stood, astonished at the height of the cedars and the entrance to the cedar forest where Humbaba walked with heavy steps. Paths were laid out and the roads well kept. They saw the cedar mountain, the dwelling of the gods, the sanctuary of Irnini. Before the mountain stood a cedar of magnificent splendor. Its shade was fine and full of gladness, sweetness, and delight. The thorns beneath the dark canopy of the vast forest were thick and tangled............
[Fragments indicate that a battle with Humbaba begins.]

'We have arrived at a place forbidden to men. Let us set our weapons against the gate of Humbaba.' Enkidu said to Gilgamesh: 'Humbaba is as violent as an oncoming storm. Like the god of storms, he will destroy us.'

Humbaba opened his mouth and said to Gilgamesh: 'Only fools would take advice from vulgar brutes. What brings you before me? Enkidu, you are the spawn of fish — a man who knows no father, the hatchling of a turtle who never suckled his mother's milk. In your youth I watched you, though I never went near. Traitor! You bring Gilgamesh before me and stand as warrior and stranger. I will cut Gilgamesh's throat and leave his body for the vultures.'
Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'My friend, the face of this monster Humbaba has changed. Even though we came to defeat him, I fear my heart will not allow it.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Why, my friend, do you speak like a coward? Your fear makes me lose faith. We have only one task before us. The copper is already running into the mold. To unleash the Flood is to crack the whip. Do not retreat! Do not pull back! Strike with everything you have!'

Gilgamesh struck the ground and charged the monster. At their feet the earth gave way. In their struggle they broke the mountains of Sirion and Lebanon. The clouds turned black and rained death upon them. Shamash unleashed all the winds against Humbaba — south, north, east, and west, the hurricane, the tempest, the typhoon, the gale, the frost-wind, the devil-wind, the blast and counterblast, and the tornado. Thirteen winds darkened Humbaba's face so that Gilgamesh could reach him with his weapons. Humbaba pleaded for his life:

'You are young, Gilgamesh, but truly a son of the wild cow Ninsun. By the command of Shamash, you have flattened the great mountains, O king of Uruk. Spare my life. Let me live out my days in the Cedar Forest. Take as many trees as you want. I will guard the wood that will be the pride of your palace.'
Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Do not listen to his pleas!'

Humbaba spoke to Enkidu: 'You know the ways of the forest, and you know the art of speech. I should have hung you from a tree and left your body for the vultures. Yet my life depends on you — tell Gilgamesh to spare me.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, slay Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest. Destroy all his power. Do this before Enlil discovers what we have done and the gods turn their anger on us — Enlil in Nippur and Shamash in Larsa. Make for us an everlasting name, because Gilgamesh slew the monstrous Humbaba.'
Humbaba lifted his head and spoke to Enkidu: 'You sit before Gilgamesh like a hired shepherd, slavishly obeying your master. Yet my life depends on you — tell Gilgamesh to spare me.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, slay Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest. Destroy all his power. Do this before Enlil discovers what we have done and the gods turn their anger on us — Enlil in Nippur and Shamash in Larsa. Make for us an everlasting name, because Gilgamesh slew the monstrous Humbaba.'
Humbaba heard everything and cursed them both: 'May neither of you live to see old age. Except by Gilgamesh, none shall bury Enkidu.'
Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'I spoke to you, my friend, but you did not hear me. Let Humbaba's curses fall back on his own head.'

Gilgamesh heard what his friend said. He drew his dagger and struck the monster's neck. Humbaba fell. Blood poured from him like rivers, filling the ravines. As he fell, he shook the ground for two leagues in every direction — the same ground he once made tremble with the thunder of his voice. Gilgamesh pulled out his tongue, his lungs, and his entrails. From the monster's head, he carved off the tusks as trophies. Abundance rained down upon the mountains. Gilgamesh discovered the secret dwelling of the gods as he trampled through the primeval forest.

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'You have felled the guardian of the forest by your strength alone. Nothing can bring you dishonor. Now — flatten the Cedar Forest. Find me a tall cedar whose tip touches the sky. I will fashion from it a door as wide as a reed-length, with no pivot — it will simply rest within the doorframe. Its thickness will be a cubit, its width a full reed-length. No stranger shall approach a door meant only for the love of the gods. The Euphrates will carry the door to the Temple of Enlil in Nippur, where the people and the god himself will rejoice in it.'
They built a raft and placed a great cedar upon it. Enkidu piloted the raft, and Gilgamesh carried the head of Humbaba.

chapters.title: Tablet VI — The Rejection of Ishtar
paragraphs: He cleaned his weapons and polished his armor. He removed his battle gear. He took off his soiled garments and put on clean robes. He dressed himself in his finest ornaments and placed the crown upon his head.

Ishtar, the great goddess, gazed upon the beauty of Gilgamesh and desired him. She said: 'Come, Gilgamesh — be my husband. Give me your strength. Be my husband and let me be your wife. I will set you in a chariot of precious stones and gold, with wheels of gold and horns of amber. You will harness great lions to pull it. Under fragrant cedars you will enter our house. When you step through the door, people will kiss your feet. Kings, lords, and rulers will bow before you. Whatever mountain and country produce, they will bring as tribute. Your sheep will bear twin lambs. Your loaded donkey will outpace the mule.
Your horse will gallop in glory before the chariot, and no ox will equal yours.'
But Gilgamesh spoke to the great goddess Ishtar:

'If I were to marry you, where would my sustenance come from? Would you feed me the food of the gods and pour me kingly ale? And who would want to marry you? You are the frost that freezes no ice. The door that blocks no wind. Bitumen that stains whoever holds it. A water-skin that cuts the hands of its carrier. Limestone that weakens the wall it builds. A battering ram that destroys the walls of allies. A shoe that blisters the foot of its wearer. Let me recite the history of your lovers. Where is your husband Dumuzi, who was supposed to be yours forever? What became of the colorful allallu-bird? I will tell you what your love has done. To Dumuzi, your youthful husband, you brought weeping and grief every year. The allallu-bird, so bright in color — you loved it, then broke its wings. Now it sits in the forest crying, "O my wing!" You loved a lion, powerful and strong, yet you dug seven pits to trap him. You loved a horse, great in battle, but with lash, spur, and whip you forced it to run seven double-leagues without rest. When it was tired and thirsty, you drove it onward — bringing tears to its mother Silili. You loved a shepherd who offered you incense daily and slaughtered lambs for your pleasure. You struck him and turned him into a wolf, so that his own sheep-boys chased him away and his own dogs tore him apart. You loved Ishullanu, your father's gardener, who brought you fruit every day and adorned your table. You looked at him and said, "Ishullanu, let us enjoy your manly strength. Reach out your hand and touch me." But Ishullanu said to you, "What do you want from me? Has my mother not baked? Have I not eaten? Should I now eat food that is nothing but insult? Should only rushes cover me against the cold?" When you heard his refusal, you struck him and turned him into a dwarf, trapping him on a bed from which he can never rise. And now you would love me — but I would end up just like them.'

When Ishtar heard these words, she was enraged. She flew up to heaven, to her father Anu and her mother Antum, and said: 'Father, Gilgamesh has insulted me! He has thrown my evil deeds in my face — my deeds of evil and violence.'
Anu spoke to the mighty goddess Ishtar: 'Did you not provoke Gilgamesh, so that he threw your evil deeds in your face — your deeds of evil and violence?'

Ishtar spoke to Anu, her father: 'Father, give me the Bull of Heaven so I can kill Gilgamesh in his own dwelling. If you do not give me the Bull of Heaven, I will smash the gates of the underworld and free the dead. I will bring up the dead to devour the living. I will make the dead outnumber those who live.'
Anu spoke to the mighty goddess Ishtar: 'If you want the Bull of Heaven, then make the widow of Uruk store seven years of wheat, and make the farmer of Uruk grow seven years of hay.'

Ishtar spoke to Anu: 'The wheat is already stored. The hay is already grown. The widow of Uruk gathered seven years of wheat. The farmer of Uruk grew seven years of hay. With the Bull of Heaven, I will have my revenge.'
Anu heard the words of the mighty goddess Ishtar and gave her the nose-rope of the Bull of Heaven.

Ishtar descended with the Bull of Heaven, leading it to Uruk. Its thirst drained the marshes and the forest dry. It lowered the river by seven cubits. When the Bull snorted, the earth cracked open and a hundred men of Uruk fell into the chasm. A second time it snorted, and two hundred men fell. A third time it snorted and the earth opened, and Enkidu fell in up to his waist. But Enkidu leaped out of the crack and seized the Bull by its horns. The Bull spat in his face.

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, we have set ourselves above others in this city. How shall we answer to the people? I have tested the Bull's strength and learned its ways. Let me test it once more. I will stand behind it and grab it by the tail. I will set my foot against its leg, and then you can slaughter it with your knife like a skilled butcher.'

Enkidu came up behind the Bull of Heaven and grabbed it by its heavy tail. He braced his foot against its leg. Then Gilgamesh slaughtered it with his knife like a skilled butcher. After they killed the Bull of Heaven, they made its heart an offering to Shamash. They bowed before the Sun God. Then Gilgamesh and Enkidu sat together.
Ishtar climbed onto the wall of Uruk. She let out a piercing cry and broke into a curse: 'Woe to Gilgamesh, who has grieved me and killed the Bull of Heaven!'
But Enkidu heard her words. He tore out the right flank of the Bull of Heaven and threw it in her face, saying: 'If I could catch you, I would do the same to you. I would drape your arm in entrails.'

Ishtar gathered her followers — the temple women and sacred prostitutes. Over the right flank of the Bull of Heaven she wept and mourned. But Gilgamesh assembled his people and all his workers. The workers admired the size of its horns. Thirty minas of precious stones they were worth. Two minas was the size of their rims. Six measures of oil they could hold. Gilgamesh dedicated the horns to his god Lugalbanda. He brought them and hung them in the shrine. Then they washed their hands in the Euphrates, took the road, and rode through the streets of Uruk. The people assembled and looked with astonishment at the heroes.

Gilgamesh spoke to the servants of his palace: 'Who is the most glorious among the heroes? Who shines brightest among men? Gilgamesh is the most glorious among the heroes! Gilgamesh shines brightest among men!'

Gilgamesh held a joyful feast in his palace. Then the heroes lay down to sleep, stretched out upon their couches. And Enkidu slept, and saw a vision in his dream. He rose in the morning, considered the dream, and spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, why have the great gods taken counsel together?'

chapters.title: Tablet VII — The Death of Enkidu
paragraphs: 'My friend, why have the great gods taken counsel together?' When dawn broke, Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'What a dream I had last night. The great gods — Anu, Enlil, Ea, and Shamash — held an assembly. Anu spoke to Enlil: "Because these two slew the Bull of Heaven and killed Humbaba, the guardian of the mountains and the Cedar Forest, one of them must die." Enlil said, "Let Enkidu die. Gilgamesh must not die." But Shamash spoke to Enlil: "Was it not by your command that they slew the Bull of Heaven and Humbaba? Why should innocent Enkidu die for this?" Enlil burned with anger at Shamash and said, "Every day you traveled with them as their companion."'

Enkidu fell before Gilgamesh and began to weep, tears flowing like rivers. 'My brother, I will never again stand before you. Once I cross the gates of the underworld, I will never set eyes upon you again.'

Enkidu lifted his eyes and began to speak to a door as though it were a man: 'Dumb door, I know what you do not. Across twenty leagues I searched for your timber until I found you, the finest of cedars. No other tree compares. Six gar is your height and two gar your width. You are a single piece — from pivot to post — a piece I raised and installed in Nippur. Had I known how you would repay my effort, I would have used my axe to cut you down and set you adrift as a raft to the temple of Shamash, who heard my words and gave me my weapon. If I raised you, perhaps I can also destroy you. May some future king despise you. May he strip my name from your wood and carve his own in its place.'
Enkidu began to weep again. As Gilgamesh listened, he wept too.

Gilgamesh spoke to Enkidu: 'Why do you speak against the fates? Your dream was profound, and it has brought great dread. Your lips buzz like flies. But the gods leave nothing to the survivor except grief. I will pray to the great gods for you. I will seek out Shamash and plead on your behalf. I will beg Anu, the father of the gods. I will pray that Enlil, the great counselor, hears my words. May Ea be open to my prayer. I will make a statue for you of endless gold.'

Enkidu spoke to Gilgamesh: 'My friend, do not waste silver or gold on me. The word of Enlil is unlike that of other gods. Whatever he commands must come to pass. Whatever he sets in place cannot be undone. This is my fate, my friend — to die before my time.'

As dawn broke, Enkidu lifted his head and offered prayers to Shamash, tears glistening in the sunlight: 'I beg you, Shamash, for my life. I curse the trapper who made me less than my friend. May his share be diminished. May his god abandon him.' Then he cursed Shamhat the temple woman: 'I curse you, Shamhat, to a dark fate. May you never know a true home or the joy of a family. May you never sit among the young women. May your finest garment fall to the ground and be stained by drunkards in the dirt. May you have no beautiful things or abundance at your table. May your bed be a rough bench. May you stand at the crossroads and lie in ruined fields. May thorns cut your feet. May everyone strike your cheek. The worker will not plaster your roof. Owls will nest in your bedroom. You made weak a man who was once pure. In the very wilderness that was my home, you made me weak.'

Shamash heard Enkidu and sent a booming voice from the sky: 'Enkidu, do not curse the woman who fed you the food of the gods, poured you kingly ale, and gave you the magnificent Gilgamesh as a companion. On a grand couch Gilgamesh will let you rest. He will place you on a seat of honor at his left hand. The kings of the earth will kiss your feet. The people of Uruk will mourn you. The nations will grieve for you. And in mourning, Gilgamesh's hair will become matted. He will wander the wilderness in the skin of a lion.'

Enkidu heard Shamash's words, and his anger quieted. 'Shamhat, let me improve your destiny instead. Governors and nobles will love you. Men a league away will slap their thighs for you. At two leagues they will shake their hair for you. Soldiers will unfasten their belts at your command and shower you with obsidian, precious stones, and gold. Jewelry will be yours. Ishtar herself will open the doors of a rich man's home to you. He will leave his wife for you, though she bore him seven children.'

But Enkidu's mind remained troubled. He turned over his thoughts and spoke to his friend: 'What a dream I had. The stars of heaven fell upon the earth. Frightened, I stood there. A man appeared, his face twisted with rage. His features were as terrifying as a Thunderbird. His hands were like a lion's paws. His nails were like an eagle's talons. He grabbed me by the hair. Though I struck at him, he overpowered me. He capsized me like a raft and crushed me beneath his feet like a bull, drowning me in his venomous spit. Save me! He struck me and turned me into a dove. He bound my arms as though they were wings.

'I descended to the house of darkness, the dwelling of the goddess Irkalla. The house from which no one who enters ever returns. The road from which there is no turning back. In that house, the inhabitants are denied light. Dust is their food. Clay is their bread. They are dressed like birds, in feathered garments. They sit in darkness with no light at all. In that house, my friend, crowns are cast on the ground. There live those who once wore crowns and ruled countries — to whom Anu and Enlil once gave roasted meat. Now cold meals are laid before them. Water from leather bottles is poured out for them. Priests and ministers dwell there. Soothsayers and enchanters live there too. Temple-anointers of the great gods are there. Etana lives there. Shakkan lives there. The queen of the underworld, Ereshkigal, lives there too. Before her kneels the scribe of the underworld. He holds a tablet and reads it aloud. Ereshkigal lifted her head and saw me.
[The rest of the dream is lost.]
'Remember me, my friend — I who endured all hardships with you. Do not forget me.'
Gilgamesh spoke: 'My friend has seen a vision the like of which none shall ever equal.'

On the day of the dream, Enkidu's strength gave way. He lay sick on his bed for twelve days. On the third and fourth days, the illness worsened. On the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth, it continued to worsen. On the eleventh and twelfth days, Enkidu lay sick on his bed. Then he called to Gilgamesh and spoke to his friend: 'My god has turned against me. I do not die as one who falls in battle. I feared a warrior's death — but a man who dies in battle earns an everlasting name. I will not fall in battle. I will earn no name.'
[The remaining lines describing Enkidu's death are lost.]

chapters.title: Tablet VIII — The Funeral of Enkidu
paragraphs: As dawn broke, Gilgamesh mourned for his friend: 'Enkidu, you were raised by the gazelle, your mother, and the donkey, your father. The wild asses of the wilderness fed you their milk. The animals taught you the pastures. May all the paths of the Cedar Forest mourn you forever. May the elders of Uruk lament you and all the people who cheered us on. May the mountains and valleys mourn you as a mother mourns her son. May the trees of the forest — cypress and cedar alike — weep for you. May all the wild creatures mourn you: the hyena, the panther, the cheetah, the stag, the jackal, the lion, the wild bull, the deer, and the ibex.

'May the holy river Ulay, where we walked in our strength, mourn you. May the pure Euphrates, whose waters we used for offerings, grieve for you. May the young men who watched us slay the Bull of Heaven cry for you. May the plowman pay tribute to you, calling out your name as he cuts his furrow.

'May the shepherd who made milk and butter for your mouth mourn you. May the shepherd boy who prepared clarified butter for you grieve. May the brewer who brewed your ale weep for you. May the temple woman who anointed you with fragrant oils mourn you. May all the people mourn you as a brother. And today, I myself will mourn you most of all.

'Hear me, young men of Uruk! Hear me, elders! I mourn for Enkidu with more passion than any hired mourning-woman. It is as though an evil gale has stolen my trusted axe, my dagger and shield, my festive robe and belt.

'My friend, you were a swift wild ass, a donkey of the mountains, a panther of the wilderness. Together we climbed mountains, slew the Bull of Heaven, and killed Humbaba in the Cedar Forest. Now you are lost in sleep. Can you hear me?'

Enkidu did not lift his head. Gilgamesh felt for his heartbeat and found none. He covered the face of his friend as one covers a bride. He circled him like an eagle. He paced like a lioness mourning her lost cubs. He tore out his curly hair and stripped off his fine clothes as though they were an abomination.

At the first light of dawn, Gilgamesh cried out to all the land: 'Blacksmith, stonecutter, coppersmith! Goldsmith, jeweler! Make a statue of my friend. Let his features be lapis lazuli. Let his skin be gold. On a grand couch I will lay you down. I will place you at the seat of honor on my left. The kings of the earth will kiss your feet. The people of Uruk will mourn you. The nations will grieve for you. And in mourning, my hair will become matted. I will wander the wilderness in the skin of a lion.'

At the first light of dawn, Gilgamesh opened his treasury and examined all the wealth within. Gold, ivory, and riches of every kind he gathered for Enkidu in abundance. [The lines describing the exact nature of the wealth are damaged.] He sacrificed fatted oxen and sheep for his friend. Shamash carried the meat to the lords of the underworld. Gilgamesh made offerings to Ishtar and Namra-sit, displayed them to Shamash, and prayed the gods would welcome Enkidu. He made offerings to Ereshkigal and Dumuzi. He made offerings to Namtar and Hushbisha. He made offerings to Quassu-tabat and Ninshuluhha. He made offerings to Bibbu and Dumuzi-abzu. All were displayed to Shamash, with prayers that the gods would welcome Enkidu and walk beside him.
[Another speaks in a broken section] '...... the judge of the Anunnaki.'
When Gilgamesh heard what was spoken, he conceived a plan to dam the river.
At the first light of dawn, Gilgamesh opened the gate and brought out a great wooden table. He filled a carnelian dish with honey and a lapis lazuli dish with butter and displayed them to Shamash.
[The rest is missing.]

chapters.title: Tablet IX — The Search for Everlasting Life
paragraphs: Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his friend Enkidu. He lay stretched out on the ground and said: 'I will die and become like Enkidu. Weeping has entered my heart. The fear of death has overtaken me, and I lie here on the ground. To find Utnapishtim, son of Ubar-Tutu, I will set out at once. At a mountain pass I arrived by night. I saw lions and was afraid. But I lifted my head to the moon god Sin and prayed. My cry reached the god, and he heard me and saved me.'

In the night he saw a vision and a dream. Lions were at play. He lifted the axe in his hand and drew the dagger from his belt. Like a javelin he threw himself among them. He wounded them, killed them, scattered them. He clothed himself in their skins and ate their flesh. Gilgamesh dug new wells for water and chased the winds.
Shamash came down in concern and spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Gilgamesh, why do you wander? The life you seek, you will never find.'

Gilgamesh said to Shamash: 'When my wandering is over and I descend to the underworld, will I not find rest there? My years there will be spent in sleep. Let my eyes drink in the sun until they have had their fill. The underworld is a land of perpetual darkness. When would the dead ever again see the glorious rays of the sun?'

He came now to the twin mountain called Mashu. Its entrance was guarded daily by monsters. Their backs reached to the vault of heaven. Their chests reached down to the underworld. Scorpion-men guarded the gate. They radiated terrible dread, and to look upon them meant death. Their splendor was fearsome enough to overthrow mountains. From sunrise to sunset, they guarded the path of the sun.

Gilgamesh saw them. Fear and terror darkened his face. His mind reeled at the wildness of their appearance. One scorpion-man said to his wife: 'The one who comes toward us — his body is the flesh of the gods.'
His wife answered: 'Two-thirds of him is god. One-third is man.'

The scorpion-man called out to Gilgamesh: 'Has a god sent you? How did you come to travel such distant roads? How did you reach me? The seas you have crossed are dangerous. How did you make the journey?'
'I seek to find Utnapishtim, my ancestor, who was taken into the assembly of the gods and given power over life and death.'

The scorpion-man spoke to Gilgamesh: 'No one before you has ever been like you, Gilgamesh. No one has ever traveled the path of the Sun God through the mountain. Twelve double-hours of total darkness in every direction must be crossed.'
[The rest of the answer and Gilgamesh's reply are fragmentary. But the hero was undaunted, and the scorpion-man agreed to his urgent request and opened the gate of the mountain.]
The scorpion-man spoke to Gilgamesh: 'Go, Gilgamesh. May the mountains of Mashu let you pass. May they watch over you and protect you. May the gates of Mashu be open to you.'

Gilgamesh heard the words of the scorpion-man and set out on the path of the Sun God. One double-hour he walked — thick was the darkness, and no light came. Two double-hours — thick was the darkness. Three double-hours — thick was the darkness. Four, five, six, seven double-hours — thick was the darkness, and no light came. At eight double-hours he quickened his pace. Still thick was the darkness. At nine double-hours, wind began to blow in his face. Still thick was the darkness. Ten double-hours — darkness. At eleven, only one double-hour of travel remained. Then at twelve double-hours, Gilgamesh emerged ahead of the sun.

There was brilliance. As he saw it, he ran toward the trees of the gods. One great tree bore fruit of carnelian, its branches hanging low — beautiful to see. Another tree bore lapis lazuli — laden with dazzling fruit. Other precious trees stood there as well. Gilgamesh reached out to touch their fruit.
As Gilgamesh wandered among the trees, a goddess lifted her head to watch him.

chapters.title: Tablet X — The Tavern at the Edge of the World
paragraphs: The tavern-keeper Siduri lived in a tavern by the sea. Her pots and stands were golden, and she wore hoods and veils upon veils. Gilgamesh approached, dressed in animal skins, fearful to look upon. His body was of the gods, but his heart was heavy with grief. His face was like that of a man who had traveled a great distance. Siduri saw him from afar and spoke to herself: 'Surely this man must be a hunter of wild bulls — but where has he come from to arrive at my gate?' When she saw him approach, she bolted the door and went up to her roof.
Gilgamesh listened, then looked up at her. He said: 'Siduri, why do you bolt the gate against me? I will break it down.'
Siduri said to Gilgamesh: 'I bolted the gate and went to my roof. Tell me about your journey.'

Gilgamesh said to Siduri: 'My friend Enkidu and I climbed mountains together. We slew the Bull of Heaven. We killed Humbaba, who lived in the Cedar Forest. We killed the lions that roamed between the mountains.'

The tavern-keeper said to Gilgamesh: 'If you truly climbed mountains, slew the Bull of Heaven, killed Humbaba in the Cedar Forest, and slew the lions between the mountains — then why are you so pale and gaunt? Why are your features sunken and hollow? Why is your face so sickly? Why is your heart heavy with grief? Why do you look like a man who has traveled a long distance? Why is your skin blasted by the weather? And why do you wander in a lion's skin?'

Gilgamesh said to the tavern-keeper: 'Why should I not be pale and gaunt? Why should my features not be sunken and hollow, my face sickly? Why should my heart not be heavy with grief? Why should I not look like one who has traveled far? Why should my skin not be blasted by the weather? Why should I not wander in a lion's skin? My friend Enkidu was a swift wild ass, a donkey of the mountains, a panther of the wilderness. He was the friend I loved more than any man. He went with me through every danger until the fate of all mortals took him. For six days and seven nights I wept over him. I left his body unburied until a maggot crawled from his nostril. Then the fear of death seized me, and I set out wandering on distant roads through the wilderness. What happened to Enkidu was too much to bear. Must I stay silent? The friend I loved has been turned to clay. Enkidu, my friend. I will not lie down like him. I will not sink to where he is now.'
Gilgamesh said to Siduri: 'Tell me — which is the way to Utnapishtim? What are the landmarks? If it is possible, I will cross the sea. If not, I will find a way across the land.'

Siduri answered Gilgamesh: 'There has never been a crossing here. No one since the beginning of time has crossed the sea. Only Shamash, the hero, crosses it. The crossing is difficult. The way is extremely dangerous. The Waters of Death seal its entrance. How, then, Gilgamesh, will you cross the sea? But there is Urshanabi, the boatman of Utnapishtim. You will find him by the stones. In the forest he fells a cedar. If you can find him, perhaps you can cross with him. If not, turn back.'

When Gilgamesh heard this, he lifted his axe, drew his dagger, and rushed down like a javelin. Urshanabi saw him coming and reached for the axe, but Gilgamesh struck him on the head and knocked him down. The Stone Men — the boat crew who were immune to the Waters of Death — took fright. Gilgamesh smashed them to pieces and threw them into the water. Then he stood over Urshanabi and stared into his eyes.
Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: 'Tell me your name. I am Urshanabi, boatman of Utnapishtim the distant.'
Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi: 'My name is Gilgamesh, from Uruk-Eanna. I found the hidden path through the mountains where the sun travels, and I followed it here.'

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: 'Why are you so pale and gaunt? Why are your features sunken and hollow? Why is your face so sickly? Why is your heart heavy with grief? Why do you look like one who has traveled far? Why is your skin blasted by the weather? Why do you wander in a lion's skin?'

Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi: 'Why should I not be pale and gaunt? Why should my features not be sunken and hollow, my face sickly? Why should my heart not be heavy with grief? Why should I not look like one who has traveled far? Why should my skin not be blasted by the weather? Why should I not wander in a lion's skin? My friend Enkidu was a swift wild ass, a donkey of the mountains, a panther of the wilderness. He was the friend I loved more than any man. He went with me through every danger until the fate of all mortals took him. For six days and seven nights I wept over him. I left his body unburied until a maggot crawled from his nostril. Then the fear of death seized me, and I set out wandering on distant roads through the wilderness. What happened to Enkidu was too much to bear. Must I stay silent? The friend I loved has been turned to clay. Enkidu, my friend. I will not lie down like him. I will not sink to where he is now.'
Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi: 'Tell me, Urshanabi, the road to Utnapishtim. What are the landmarks? If it is possible, I will cross the sea. If not, I will turn back.'

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: 'Your own hand has prevented the crossing, Gilgamesh. You smashed the Stone Men and threw them into the river. Without them the crossing cannot be made. Now take the axe at your side. Go into the forest and cut three hundred punting-poles, each five gar long. Trim and smooth each one and bring them to me.'

Gilgamesh heard this, took the axe at his side, drew his dagger, and went into the forest. He cut three hundred punting-poles, each five gar long. He smeared them with pitch and brought them to Urshanabi. Then Gilgamesh and Urshanabi set out together.
The ship tossed to and fro as they traveled. A journey of forty-five days they completed in three. Urshanabi brought them to the Waters of Death.

Urshanabi said to Gilgamesh: 'Take the first punting-pole. Do not let your hands touch the Waters of Death, or they will wither. Take the second pole, then a third, then a fourth. Take the fifth, the sixth, the seventh. Take the eighth, a ninth, a tenth. Take the eleventh, and the twelfth.'
After six score double-furlongs, all the punting-poles were spent. Urshanabi removed his robes and Gilgamesh removed his garments. From them, Urshanabi fashioned a sail.

Utnapishtim, watching from the distance, thought to himself: 'Why are the Stone Men of the ship destroyed? And someone who is not the ship's master rides in it. The one who comes is no man of mine. On the right side...... I look......
I look...... I look...... The one who comes is no man of mine.'
Gilgamesh drew near the shore and spoke to Utnapishtim: 'Utnapishtim, you who survived the Great Flood......' [The rest is lost.]

Utnapishtim said to Gilgamesh: 'Why are you so pale and gaunt? Why are your features sunken and hollow? Why is your face so sickly? Why is your heart heavy with grief? Why do you look like one who has traveled far? Why is your skin blasted by the weather? Why do you wander in a lion's skin?'

Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim: 'Why should I not be pale and gaunt? Why should my features not be sunken and hollow, my face sickly? Why should my heart not be heavy with grief? Why should I not look like one who has traveled far? Why should my skin not be blasted by the weather? Why should I not wander in a lion's skin? My friend Enkidu was a swift wild ass, a donkey of the mountains, a panther of the wilderness. He was the friend I loved more than any man. He went with me through every danger until the fate of all mortals took him. For six days and seven nights I wept over him. I left his body unburied until a maggot crawled from his nostril. Then the fear of death seized me, and I set out wandering on distant roads through the wilderness. What happened to Enkidu was too much to bear. Must I stay silent? The friend I loved has been turned to clay. Enkidu, my friend. I will not lie down like him. I will not sink to where he is now.'

Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim: 'I have come here, and now I will see Utnapishtim, whom people call the distant one. I have traveled through all lands. I have crossed steep mountains. I have crossed every sea. I had little sleep. I denied myself rest. I have filled my body with grief — all in vain. Before I reached the tavern-keeper, my clothes had worn away. I killed wild beasts — the hyena, the panther, the cheetah, the stag, the jackal, the lion, the wild bull, the deer, and the ibex. I ate their flesh and wore their pelts. But now — let the gates of sorrow be sealed tight with tar and pitch. Let sorrow never again interrupt my joy.'

Utnapishtim said to Gilgamesh: 'Why do you chase after sorrows? You are made of the stuff of gods — fashioned from divine and human flesh in the image of your father and mother. Have you compared your lot to that of the fool? The fool eats spoiled yeast, not fresh butter. He eats bran and grist, not milled flour. He wears rags, not fine robes. He ties old rope, not a proper belt. [Portions that follow are fragmentary and describe the actions of the gods.] Enkidu the gods have indeed brought to his doom. But what have you gained from your suffering? As you exhaust yourself and drain your strength, you only hasten the end of your own days. A man's life can snap like a dry reed. The handsome young man and the beautiful young woman — both may fall to Death too soon. No one sees Death. No one hears his voice. Yet Death reaps us all.

'As long as houses are built, as long as contracts are sealed, as long as brothers quarrel, as long as strife and hatred exist in the land, as long as the river carries water to the sea — for just that long, there is no portrait of death ever drawn. The dead never greet the living. The great gods, the Anunnaki, assemble. Mammitum, the goddess of destiny, sits with them. Together they determine death and life. But the days of death are never revealed to mankind.'

chapters.title: Tablet XI — The Story of the Flood
paragraphs: Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim: 'I gaze at you in amazement, Utnapishtim. You look no different from me. Your nature is the same as mine, though you have departed this life. Yet my heart still struggles against what no longer burdens you. Tell me — how did you come to dwell here and gain eternal life among the gods?'

Utnapishtim said to Gilgamesh: 'I will reveal a hidden story to you, Gilgamesh. I will tell you a mystery of the gods. The city of Shuruppak — a city you know, sitting on the banks of the Euphrates — was very old, and so were the gods within it. The great gods, as many as they were, decided to bring a flood. Their father Anu, their counselor Enlil the warrior, their leader Ninurta, and their champion Ennugi — all agreed. But Ea, the lord of unfathomable wisdom, argued against it. He told their plan to a reed hut, saying:

'"Reed hut, reed hut! Clay wall, clay wall! Reed hut, hear me. Clay wall, pay attention. Man of Shuruppak, son of Ubara-Tutu — build a house, build a ship. Abandon your possessions. Save your life. Give up your goods and save living things. Bring the seed of every living creature into the ship. As for the ship you will build, let its measurements be carefully proportioned — its width and length in proper balance. Then launch it on the sea."'
'I understood, and said to Ea, my lord:',
'"I will do as you command, my lord. I will carry out your order. But what shall I tell the people of the city, and the elders?"'
'Ea spoke again and said to me, his servant:',

'"Tell them this: 'I know that Enlil hates me. I can no longer live in your city. I cannot remain safely on Enlil's land. I will descend to the Apsu and live with Ea, my lord. Upon you he will pour rich blessings — fowl in plenty and fish in abundance, herds of cattle and a great harvest. In the morning he will rain down bread for you. In the evening, a shower of wheat.'"'

'As soon as dawn appeared, the people gathered at my gate. The carpenter came with his hatchet. The reed-worker came with his flattening-stone. Everyone assembled. The rich men brought pitch. The poor men gathered everything else that was needed.',

'On the fifth day I set the hull in place. It covered an acre. Its sides were ten gar high, and ten gar across the deck. I built it in six stories, making seven floors. The interior of each floor I divided into nine rooms. I cut beaks for water drainage. I selected a punting-pole and added everything necessary. Three measures of pitch I smeared on the outside. Three measures of asphalt I used inside to make it watertight. Three measures of oil the workers carried in vessels. One measure of oil I kept aside for sacrifices. The other two the boatman stored away. I slaughtered oxen and killed lambs day after day. I gave the workers beer, oil, and sweet wine freely, as if it were river water — a feast like the New Year. I brought oil before Shamash. The ship was completed. The launching was difficult, and I added tackle above and below until the ship sank two-thirds into the water.',

'With everything I owned, I filled it. With all my silver, I filled it. With all my gold, I filled it. With every living creature, I filled it. Then I brought aboard all my family and relatives, the cattle of the field, the beasts of the field, and all the righteous people. Shamash had set a time: "When the rulers of darkness send a destructive rain at evening, enter the ship and shut its door." That sign came. The rulers of darkness sent a destructive rain at evening. I saw the storm approaching and was afraid. I entered the ship and shut the door.',

'I entrusted the ship to Puzur-Amurri, the boatman, along with the great vessel and all its cargo. At the first light of dawn, a black cloud rose on the horizon. Within it, the storm god Adad thundered. His heralds, Shullat and Hanish, went ahead across mountain and plain. The gods of the abyss rose up. Nergal tore loose the dams of the deep. Ninurta caused the riverbanks to overflow. The Anunnaki raised their torches high, and their brightness lit the entire world. The storm sent by Adad reached up to heaven. All light turned to darkness. Adad shattered the land like a clay pot.',

'The storm blew with such violence for a whole day that it submerged the mountains. It rushed in on the people like an onslaught of battle. No brother could see his brother. The people could not be seen from heaven. Even the gods were afraid of the storm. They retreated to the highest heaven of Anu. There they crouched like dogs, cowering against the walls.',

'Ishtar cried out like a woman in labor. The lady of the gods wailed in a loud voice: "The world of old has turned back to clay, because I agreed to this evil in the assembly of the gods. When I consented to this destruction, I was destroying my own people. What I created — where is it? Like the spawn of fish, it fills the sea." The gods wailed with her over the Anunnaki. They sat bowed down and weeping. Their lips were pressed together in fear and terror.',

'For six days and nights, the wind, storm, and tempest overwhelmed the land. When the seventh day came, the tempest, the storm, and the battle that had raged like a great host began to die down. The sea grew quiet. The hurricane and flood subsided. I looked out upon the sea and raised my voice loudly, but all of humankind had turned back into clay. The surrounding sea became as flat as a rooftop.

'I opened the hatch and light fell on my face. Stunned, I sank down and wept. Tears streamed down my cheeks. I looked in every direction — nothing but sea. I searched in vain for land. But twelve leagues distant, a strip of land rose from the water. The ship drifted to Mount Nisir. On Mount Nisir it stuck fast and did not drift. The first day, the second day — the mountain held the ship. The third day, the fourth day — it held. The fifth day, the sixth day — it held. When the seventh day came, I sent out a dove. The dove flew back and forth, but finding no place to rest, she returned. Then I sent out a swallow, but she too came back. Then I sent out a raven. The raven flew away and saw that the waters were receding. She settled down to feed. She went away and did not return.'

'I let everything go to the four winds and made a sacrifice. I poured a libation on the mountain peak. I set up seven censers and heaped into them calamus, cedarwood, and sweet incense. The gods smelled the fragrance. The gods smelled the sweet fragrance. They gathered like flies around the sacrifice. When the lady of the gods arrived, she lifted the great necklace that Anu had made for her and said:',

'"You gods here — by my lapis lazuli necklace, I will not forget. I will remember these days forever. Let the gods come to the offering. But Enlil shall not come, because he rashly brought the flood and handed my people over to destruction."'
'When Enlil arrived and saw the ship, he was furious. Rage filled his heart against the gods: "Who has survived? No man was to escape the destruction!"'
'Ninurta spoke to Enlil the warrior: "Who but Ea could have planned this? Does Ea not know all things?"'
'Ea spoke to Enlil the warrior:',

'"You — wise one among the gods, warrior — how rash of you to send the flood. Punish the sinner for his sins. Punish the wicked for their wickedness. But show mercy. Do not destroy everyone. Instead of a flood, send lions to thin mankind. Instead of a flood, send tigers. Instead of a flood, send famine. Instead of a flood, send plague. I did not betray the secret of the great gods. I only let Utnapishtim see it in a dream. That is how he learned the mystery of the gods."'

'Enlil arrived at a decision. He came aboard the ship, took me by the hand, and led me out. He led out my wife as well and made her kneel beside me. Standing between us, he turned us to face each other and blessed us: "Before this day, Utnapishtim was only human. But now Utnapishtim and his wife shall be like gods. Let Utnapishtim live far away from men, at the mouth of the rivers."'
'Then they took us away and settled us far off, at the mouth of the rivers.'

After Utnapishtim finished this account, he turned to Gilgamesh and said: 'Now — who among the gods will give you the strength to gain the life you desire? Let me test you. Try not to sleep.' And for six days and seven nights, Gilgamesh lay as still as a dead man. Sleep had fallen on him like a storm. Utnapishtim said to his wife: 'Look at this hero who wants to live forever. Sleep has fallen on him like a storm.' His wife replied: 'Touch him. Wake him. Let him return to his land in health. Let him go back through the great door to his own country.' Utnapishtim said: 'All men are deceivers, and this one will deceive you too. Bake loaves for him. Place one by his head each day. And mark the days he sleeps upon the wall.'

While Gilgamesh slept, she baked the loaves and placed one at his head and marked the wall. The first loaf went hard. The second turned leathery. The third went soggy. The fourth turned white. The fifth grew gray with mold. The sixth was still fresh. The seventh — just then, Utnapishtim touched him and he woke.

Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim: 'I must have drifted off — and then you touched me and I woke.' Utnapishtim said to Gilgamesh: 'Count the loaves. Look at the marks on the wall. The first is hard. The second is leathery. The third is soggy. The fourth is white. The fifth is gray with mold. The sixth is fresh. The seventh was still warm when I touched you and you woke.'
Gilgamesh said to Utnapishtim: 'What shall I do? Where shall I go? A demon has seized my body. Death sits on my bed. Wherever my foot steps, there is death.'

Utnapishtim spoke to Urshanabi the boatman: 'Urshanabi, this harbor rejects you now. The boat must carry you away. You are forever banished from this place. The man before you is covered in filth. The wild skins he wears have hidden the beauty of his body. Take him to the place of cleansing. Let him wash his hair until it is clean as snow. Let him cast off his skins and the sea will carry them away. His body will appear beautiful again. Replace the band on his head. Give him a garment to cover his nakedness. Until he reaches his city and his journey's end, the garment will not age. It will stay entirely new.'

Urshanabi took Gilgamesh to the place of cleansing. He washed his hair until it was clean as snow. He cast off his skins, and the sea carried them away. His body appeared beautiful once more. Urshanabi replaced the band on his head and gave him a garment to cover his nakedness. It would not age or wear out until he reached his city.

Gilgamesh and Urshanabi boarded the ship once more, and it tossed to and fro as they traveled. Utnapishtim's wife spoke to her husband: 'Gilgamesh came here weary and exhausted. What will you give him so he can return to his country?'
Gilgamesh raised the pole and drew the boat near the shore.

Utnapishtim spoke to Gilgamesh: 'You came here weary and suffering. What shall I give you for your journey home? I will reveal a mystery of the gods. There is a plant that looks like buckthorn. Its thorn stings like a bramble. If your hands can reach that plant, your hands will hold what gives eternal life.'

Gilgamesh heard this and opened the sluice gates so the current would carry him into the deep. He tied heavy stones to his feet, which dragged him down to the sea floor. There he found the plant. He grasped the prickly thing. He cut the stones from his feet, and the sea rose and threw him upon the shore.

Gilgamesh said to Urshanabi: 'This plant is a thing of wonder. By it, a man can regain his youth. I will take it to Uruk, the great-walled city. I will give it to the old men to eat. Its name shall be: "Even the old man becomes young again." I will eat it myself and return to the strength of my youth.'

At twenty double-leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty double-leagues they stopped to rest. Gilgamesh spotted a pool of cool water. He stepped in to bathe. A serpent smelled the sweetness of the plant and darted out. It snatched the plant away. As it turned back toward the water, it shed its skin. Gilgamesh sat down and wept. Tears ran down his face. He said to Urshanabi the boatman:

'Why did my hands tremble? Why did my heart stand still? I gained nothing for myself. The benefit went to a snake. Already the water has carried the plant twenty double-leagues away. I opened the sluice and lowered my tools to find it. What I found has become a sign — and an omen. I must go home and leave the ship behind on the shore.'

They continued on. At twenty double-leagues they stopped to eat. At thirty double-leagues they stopped to rest. When they arrived at Uruk, the great-walled city, Gilgamesh spoke to Urshanabi the boatman:

'Urshanabi — climb up and walk along the wall of Uruk. Inspect the cornerstone. Examine the brickwork. See if the wall is not made of fired brick, its foundation laid by the Seven Sages. One-third is city. One-third is garden. One-third is field. And there is a precinct for the temple of Ishtar. These parts and the precinct make up the whole of Uruk.'

chapters.title: Tablet XII — Enkidu and the Netherworld
paragraphs: 'If only I had left my ball at the carpenter's shop! O wife of the carpenter, you who were like a mother to me — if only I had left it there. O daughter of the carpenter, you who were like a sister — if only I had left it. Today, my ball and my mallet have fallen down to the underworld.'
Enkidu answered Gilgamesh: 'Do not weep, my master. This very day I will go down to the underworld and bring back your mallet and your ball.'

Gilgamesh answered Enkidu: 'If you are going to the underworld, you must hear my advice. Do not wear clean clothes, or you will be marked as a stranger. Do not anoint yourself with sweet-smelling oil, or the dead will crowd around you, drawn by the scent. Do not stretch a bow upon the ground, or those slain by arrows will gather around you. Do not carry a staff, or the spirits of death will tremble before you. Do not tie sandals to your feet. Do not shout a war cry above ground. Do not kiss the wife you loved. Do not strike the wife you hated. Do not kiss the son you loved. Do not strike the son you hated. The sorrows of the netherworld have overtaken you — and her who is dark, she who is dark, mother Ninazu, whose gleaming white body is clothed in no garment, whose breasts are bare like stone.'

But when Enkidu went down to the underworld, he ignored every piece of Gilgamesh's advice. He dressed in clean clothes, and was marked as a stranger. He anointed himself with sweet oil, and the dead gathered around him. He stretched a bow upon the ground, and those slain by arrows gathered about him. He carried a staff, and the spirits trembled. He tied sandals to his feet. He shouted a war cry. He kissed the wife he loved. He struck the wife he hated. He kissed the son he loved. He struck the son he hated. The sorrows of the netherworld overtook him — and her who is dark, she who is dark, mother Ninazu, whose gleaming white body is clothed in no garment, whose breasts are bare like stone.

From the netherworld, Enkidu cried out to the world above. Namtar had not seized him. Disease had not seized him. The netherworld itself had seized him. The merciless demon of Nergal had not seized him. The netherworld itself had seized him. He had not fallen on the battlefield. The netherworld had simply seized him.

Gilgamesh went alone to the House of Enlil and prayed: 'Father Enlil, my ball has fallen into the netherworld, and my mallet has fallen in as well. Enkidu went down to retrieve them, but the netherworld has seized him. Namtar did not seize him. Disease did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. The merciless demon of Nergal did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. He did not fall in battle. The netherworld simply seized him.' Father Enlil did not answer.

Gilgamesh went alone to the House of Sin and prayed: 'Father Sin, my ball has fallen into the netherworld, and my mallet has fallen in as well. Enkidu went down to retrieve them, but the netherworld has seized him. Namtar did not seize him. Disease did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. The merciless demon of Nergal did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. He did not fall in battle. The netherworld simply seized him.' Father Sin did not answer.

Gilgamesh went alone to the Temple of Enki and prayed: 'Father Enki, my ball has fallen into the netherworld, and my mallet has fallen in as well. Enkidu went down to retrieve them, but the netherworld has seized him. Namtar did not seize him. Disease did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. The merciless demon of Nergal did not seize him. The netherworld seized him. He did not fall in battle. The netherworld simply seized him.'
Father Enki heard him and spoke to the hero Shamash: 'Break open the chamber of the grave. Open the ground, so that the spirit of Enkidu may rise from the earth like a wind.'

Shamash heard this prayer. He broke open the chamber of the grave and opened the ground. The spirit of Enkidu rose from the earth like a wind. Gilgamesh and Enkidu embraced and kissed one another. They shared their thoughts and their questions.
'Tell me, my friend — tell me. The appearance of the land of the dead, which you have seen — tell me.'
But Enkidu replied: 'I cannot tell you, my friend. I cannot. If I were to describe the land I have seen, you would sit down and weep.'
Gilgamesh said: 'Then let me sit down and weep.'
'Everything that once gladdened your heart is now bitter and sad. My body is like an old garment eaten by worms. Everything that once brought you joy is cloaked in dust.'
'Woe!' cried Gilgamesh, and threw himself to the ground.
'Woe!' cried Enkidu, and threw himself to the ground.

'Did you see the man with one son?' 'I saw him. He weeps over a peg fixed in his wall.' 'Did you see the man with two sons?' 'I saw him. He eats bread atop two bricks.' 'Did you see the man with three sons?' 'I saw him. He drinks water from a saddle.' 'Did you see the man with four sons?' 'I saw him. His heart rejoices like a man with a team of donkeys.' 'Did you see the man with five sons?' 'I saw him. He enters the palace with the ease of a scribe.' 'Did you see the man with six sons?' 'I saw him. He sits enthroned among the lesser gods in the assembly.' 'Did you see the man with no son?' 'I saw him. He eats bread as hard as a kiln-fired brick.' 'Did you see the eunuch of the palace?' 'I saw him. He stands in the corner like a post.'

'Did you see the man struck by the mooring pole?' 'I saw him. Woe to his mother and father — when the pegs are pulled out, he wanders.' 'Did you see the man who died before his time?' 'I saw him. He rests on a soft couch and drinks pure water.' 'Did you see the hero slain in battle?' 'I saw him. His father and mother honor his memory, and his wife weeps for him. The spirit of such a man is at rest.' 'Did you see the man whose body lies unburied in the field?' 'I saw him. His spirit finds no rest in the underworld.' 'Did you see the man whose spirit has no one left to care for it?' 'I saw him. He eats the dregs of the bowl. He eats the broken scraps of food that are cast into the street.'
